item.title: Re: @psul re: An Impenitent Thief ;>
item.content:encoded:
Thanks for reading it, Eta, and for the kind words.

Characterization of Sandra Dee: done beautifully

It's funny - I seem to have written more female than male protagonists (4 out of my 6 tales with single protagonists, plus the lead in my most tale-like SCP). It's not necessarily deliberately planned, so I'm not sure why it's happened. Certainly writing in first-person was a big challenge for me, as was trying to get inside Sandra's head, so I'm pleased when people like the result.

+1, and how, as Dr. Spanko would say.

As I commented on A Convincing Lyre, I'm a bit surprised that no-one has brought up the fact that apparently a deaf guy and a kid re-contained Dr Spanko (and the other SCPs that breached) off-screen with little fuss. If anyone would like to write the tale of how Mike Carter convinced Spanko to get back into containment, I'd love to read it!

item.title: @psul re: An Impenitent Thief ;>

+1, and how, as Dr. Spanko would say.

item.title: @MZambia re: An Impenitent Thief
item.content:encoded:
It makes no sense for a story to be told in the present, so it comes off as being different for the sake of being different.

I'm always surprised by this opinion whenever I encounter it.
IMO, all the aspects of language (mostly written, but not only…) are tools for writing. Punctuation. Spelling. Grammar. Choice of words. Pauses. Creating paragraphs. Using short, incomplete sentences, like I'm doing now. And of course, verb tenses.
Writing a story in present tense gives it a sense of timelessness and urgency. It also tends to grab the reader better, because it gives them the impression that the story is happening NOW, CLOSE, = no big step to feel the story is happening to them. It is completely different from a story told in the past, = distance, water under the bridge, to other people, etc.
I tell you verily, my friend, we writers can be a bunch of manipulative assholes!! ;>
So yes, IMO, this particular story could ONLY be told in the present tense.

ETA:

You generally only tell stories about things that have already happened.

Oh - then all science-fiction stories should be told in the future?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm moving more and more away from the idea that the Foundation has human test subjects and/or captive personnel. So it's becoming increasingly difficult for me to get into narratives that explore D-Class or any of the issues surrounding them. That's nothing to do with the author or the piece, really, but it does figure into my enjoyment of something, and therefore my vote.

Nevertheless, this hits enough points in terms of technical merit that I have no issue supporting the piece. It's a good, old-fashioned containment breach, presented in such a manner that there is a sense of consequence for the characters involved, and therefore dramatic tension. The attention to detail with things like the blinking system and the fabric ties on the suits are nice touches, and indicative of the sense of immersion that this tale achieves. Good piece of writing, and we need more of those around here.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Thanks for replying.

You generally only tell stories about things that have already happened. Thus, past tense. I guess informal anecdotes often get told in the present tense, but this certainly doesn't read like one of those.

I guess I just see things differently. I can't bring myself to think of an entire style of writing as "wrong", or as only good within an informal context. I agree that it might be harder to write in the present tense well, though, but here I think psul pulled it off nicely. Basically, to me, any style can yield good results, as long as it is appropriate to the story or the subject matter. But, to each his/her own, I guess.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm sorry that you didn't enjoy this, MZambia. I'm not trying to change your mind with the explanation below, but I think it's useful for authors to talk about why they made the choices they did.

I guess informal anecdotes often get told in the present tense, but this certainly doesn't read like one of those.

You're right - this is intended more to be a verbal capture of an internal monologue / train of thought. I haven't gone the full Virginia Woolf on it, but I think that brains tend to experience the world (and to have thoughts) in the present tense.

As to whether the rhetorical questions form a natural train of thought, I agree that those are included more to emphasise Sandra's complicated emotions about her situation, rather than representing the precise way she would think to herself. I will consider taking them out, or amending them, post-contest period - it's the question of whether the emotions will still come through.

On the reference to the biblical thieves, again this is somewhat of an artifact, so I can understand if it feels jarring. My out-of-universe justification is that I need to have a couple of mentions of SCP-012 to ensure that the last line is relevant. My in-universe justification is that actually Sandra's earlier thought about Emma talking about 012 has been percolating subconsciously, leading to the thought about biblical thieves popping up. I know that the impenitent thief joined in with the general mocking of Jesus (I wasn't aware of a specific statement), but I decided that Sandra wouldn't remember that.

And as for letting your mind wander while in charge of an extremely dangerous object - have you ever driven on a highway?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like the concept of the story overall, but I can't stand stories written in the present tense. It makes no sense for a story to be told in the present, so it comes off as being different for the sake of being different. Which, honestly, I suspect it usually is.

Also, these two lines

What do you call something that you pick up off the street, and adopt, and give it a new name and a place to sleep? Right: a stray.

What do you call a group of people that you mostly can't stand, but they're the only people who really know you, and you owe them everything? Oh yeah: family.‎

seem really forced and out of place to me. They don't feel at all like a natural train of thought and more like the author trying insert commentary. And this paragraph

There were thieves in the bible, I remember suddenly. Two of them, crucified with Jesus. One of them asked Jesus for forgiveness, the little ass-kisser. The other one didn't say anything. Did he have any regrets? I wonder what he thought about, nailed up on a cross for everyone to look at and gossip about. Up on Mount Golgotha. Funny, that's the name of 012 as well.

is even more jarring. It just reads like the author had an idea for fancy biblical symbolism and just shoved it in. All three also suffer from the problem of why a person running careful tests on an extremely dangerous object is letting her mind wander. (and, as an aside, the impenitent thief did say something)

So I guess that leaves me at -1.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm very pleased that you like this.

the way Dee contains the skip using her suit was pretty clever

As cliche as it sounds, this was as close as I've ever come to a character writing the story for me. When I started writing, I knew that I wanted things to go wrong, and to try to increase the tension towards the end, and to have *something* almost fall and make a sound, but I didn't know the exact details. I maintain that using the suit was Dee's idea.

And once that idea struck, a lot of other things fell into place:

  • the fact that taking off the suit removes the last paratech advantage that Dee has, increasing her vulnerability
  • the fact that it could be something stuffed inside a pocket of the uniform that would fall - ie it's not a factor of a poorly designed suit
  • the idea that something stuffed inside the uniform could be something stolen, helping me refer back to theft and justify the title

item.title: MTF Contest - Sequel
item.content:encoded:
In this follow-up to A Convincing Lyre, Mobile Task Force Eta-11 ("Savage Beasts") is dealing with a containment breach by SCP-339. Agent "Sandra Dee" is pretty independent, but sometimes even the best soloists need a little accompaniment.

Thanks again to my team for the MTF Contest, the Site-19 String Quartet– WrongJohnSilver, CumaeanSibyl and Smapti. Many thanks also to Hercules Rockefeller and MrWrong for review and feedback on the forums.

If you haven't found all of the MTF Eta-11 contest entries yet, below is a recommended reading order:

  • A Convincing Lyre
  • An Impenitent Thief
  • Project Proposal 2014-2112: "Dreams of Failure"
  • SCP-2402
  • Enjoy the Silence
  • The Musical Suspects
